title: Lucy v. Zehmer
summary: The sellers’ words and conduct reasonably conveyed a serious land sale, so an undisclosed intention to joke did not defeat enforcement.
notes: Court: Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia (1954), the name Virginia’s highest court used until 1971. Casebooks and citators often call it the Supreme Court of Virginia.

sections.Parties: W.O. Lucy and his brother J.C. Lucy sought specific performance against A.H. Zehmer and his wife Ida. W.O. had transferred a half interest in the proposed purchase to his brother.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties discussed the sale of the 471.6-acre Ferguson farm for $50,000 while drinking at Zehmer’s restaurant. The discussion lasted forty minutes or more. Zehmer wrote an agreement on a restaurant receipt. Lucy objected to a draft framed as “I” because he wanted both spouses bound; the writing was rewritten and both Zehmers signed. The final instrument identified the farm and price and made title satisfactory to the buyer. The parties also discussed what property the sale included.

Lucy took the writing, arranged the next day for his brother to provide half the purchase money, and hired a lawyer to examine title. Zehmer later said the transaction was a joke or bluff intended to expose Lucy’s inability to pay. His whispered statement to his wife that it was a joke was deliberately kept from Lucy. The evidence did not establish intoxication sufficient to prevent comprehension, and counsel conceded that defense at argument.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed the purchasers’ bill for specific performance after depositions. The Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed and remanded for entry of a decree requiring performance.
sections.Issue: Did a seller’s alleged private intention to joke or bluff prevent a contract where the other party honestly and reasonably understood the signed transaction as serious?
sections.Holding: No. On this record, the outward manifestations supported a binding agreement and specific performance. Lucy both believed the transaction serious and was warranted in that belief.
sections.Reasoning:
The court considered the full exchange rather than a signature in isolation. Lengthy negotiation, redrafting to bind both owners, discussion of title and included property, signatures, and Lucy’s possession of the writing all supported a serious commercial transaction. Lucy’s prompt arrangements for financing and title examination supported his own understanding.

The objective approach protects the reasonable meaning of communicated words and acts. A private reservation that the other party neither knows nor has reason to understand cannot defeat that meaning. The opinion nevertheless retains a role for actual knowledge: a party who knows the other’s unusual meaning cannot simply insist on the ordinary meaning to manufacture assent. Nor would an obviously absurd or mutually understood joke necessarily be enforceable.

The court separately rejected the attempt to invalidate the transaction for intoxication and addressed the evidence about delivery. Even accepting some of the sellers’ account, the indication of joking came only after the signed instrument had been taken. The result rests on the transaction’s objectively serious appearance and Lucy’s justified understanding, not a rule that every signed writing is enforceable regardless of circumstances.

Court: Supreme Court of Virginia (1954).

The reproduced restaurant receipt at printed p. 173 is available in the embedded page reader and was visually inspected. Its informal physical form is part of the factual context; the legal analysis still depends on the communicated undertaking and surrounding conduct.

sections.Parties: W. O. Lucy and his brother J. C. Lucy sought specific performance against A. H. and Ida Zehmer. W. O. had transferred a half interest in the purchase to his brother.
sections.Material Facts: After a prolonged conversation at the Zehmers’ restaurant, A. H. wrote an agreement to sell the 471.6-acre Ferguson farm for $50,000, with title satisfactory to the buyer. The writing changed to include both spouses, and both signed. The Zehmers later claimed the transaction was a joke and relied on drinking during the discussion. Lucy treated the agreement as serious, arranged the purchase, and obtained legal attention to title.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court denied specific performance. The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed and remanded with directions to require performance. The appellate presentation did not establish intoxication sufficient to defeat capacity.
sections.Issue: Could a party avoid the agreement through an undisclosed intention to joke when the other party actually and reasonably understood the words and conduct as a serious transaction?
sections.Holding: No. The outward agreement and its circumstances supported enforcement. Lucy reasonably believed the transaction genuine.
sections.Reasoning: The court uses the parties’ manifested meaning, including the length of discussion, revision of the writing, the wife’s signature, and the title provision. Undisclosed reservations do not displace the reasonable meaning communicated to the other party. This does not make knowledge irrelevant: a recipient who knows the speaker is joking cannot claim the same reasonable understanding. The surrounding notes therefore contrast Keller’s mutual frolic and Leonard’s objectively implausible advertisement.

learning.why: Lucy supplies the basic method for interpreting assent: identify what was communicated, what the recipient understood, and whether that understanding was justified.

topics.assent: Words and conduct reasonably communicated agreement.
topics.objective-assent: An undisclosed joke does not defeat a reasonable understanding of serious assent.
topics.intent-bound: The circumstances indicated a legally significant transaction.
topics.specific-performance: The court directed enforcement of the land-sale obligation.
